findings.description: The inline policy grants full wildcard actions on ec2, s3, lambda and cloudwatch against "Resource": "*", violating least privilege. Compromise of this user's credentials allows an attacker to read/delete all S3 data, launch or terminate any EC2 instance, and modify or backdoor any Lambda function, including privilege escalation via lambda:UpdateFunctionCode / ec2 instance profile abuse.

A permanent IAM access key is generated in Terraform without a PGP key, so the plaintext secret is stored unencrypted in the Terraform state file. Anyone with read access to state obtains long-lived credentials carrying the broad ec2/s3/lambda/cloudwatch permissions attached to this user.
The access key secret is exposed through the 'secret' Terraform output without the sensitive = true flag, so the value is printed to the console and CI/CD logs on every apply.

Permissions are attached directly to a long-lived IAM user via an inline user policy rather than through a group or an assumable role with temporary credentials, which weakens centralised access control and auditability of the wildcard privileges granted.
